result:
You have never seen your own face. Not once, not ever. Every glimpse has been mediated: mirrors reverse you, photographs flatten you, videos lag behind the moment they capture. The face you know best is a reconstruction assembled from secondhand evidence, while everyone else in your life has seen the original directly, thousands of times.

This is a small strangeness we all share and almost never discuss. You are the only person who cannot look at yourself the way others do. When you smile, you feel muscles contract; when they smile at you, you see light shift across skin. Your self-image is built from this mismatch—internal sensation stitched to external fragments—which might explain why so many of us flinch at candid photos. *That isn't me*, we say, though it is precisely us, seen without our supervision.

There's something democratic about this blindness. Everyone carries the same gap between their inner experience and their visible surface. The confident stranger on the train is also guessing at their own expression. We spend enormous energy managing how we appear while remaining fundamentally unable to verify the result.

Maybe that's why mirrors hold such quiet power—not vanity, exactly, but the novelty of catching a glimpse of the stranger we present to the world. And maybe the kindest thing we can offer each other is description: telling someone what we saw when they laughed, or cried, or thought no one was watching. Filling in, piece by piece, the face they'll never meet.
